This car, verified

We ran this car's VIN through the same decode logic behind our Cutover tool, then cross-checked it against NHTSA's own public database. Both agree on every field that overlaps: Fremont-built, model year 2024, Dual Motor AWD. Here's the breakdown, position by position.

What the VIN says

FieldWhat it decodes toWhere it lives in the VIN
Manufacturer block7SAYGAEE8Positions 1–9 (WMI + vehicle descriptor)
Check digitValid (passes the mod-11/SAE check)Position 9
Drivetrain / motorE → AWD Dual MotorPosition 8
Model yearR → 2024Position 10
Assembly plantF → Fremont, CAPosition 11
Serial number169,869Positions 12–17

NHTSA's official decode agrees

We pulled the same VIN through NHTSA's free public vPIC decoder, the U.S. government's own database, independent of anything Tesla or we calculated by hand. It confirms Make (Tesla), Model (Model Y), Model Year (2024), Plant (Fremont, California, USA), and drive configuration (Dual Motor): a clean match on every field it covers, plus a passing check-digit validation, meaning this VIN is well-formed and untampered.

One gap, not a disagreement: NHTSA's database doesn't carry Tesla-specific detail like battery pack size or Long Range vs. Performance trim. That's a known limitation of the public database, not an error. Trim confirmation (Long Range specifically) comes from your Tesla account and window sticker, not NHTSA.

HW3 vs. HW4: which one you have

Fremont's Model Y line switched from Autopilot HW3 to HW4 hardware around a serial-number window in 2023. Your car is a full model year (2024) past that transition and doesn't fall inside the ambiguous window at all: this is HW4, high confidence, no serial-number lookup required. If you ever want to check a different VIN (a friend's car, one you're shopping), that's exactly what our Cutover tool does: same decode logic, VIN in, answer out.

This car's own screen puts it to rest. Under Software → Additional Vehicle Information, it reads "AI Computer: Full Self-Driving Computer 4." Straight from the car, no VIN math required. Even the car's own nickname in the Tesla app matches this page's name.

The car's own screen, confirming HW4 directly.

Wheels

Long Range AWD offered exactly two wheel choices in 2024, no 18" or 21" option on this trim (21" Überturbine wheels are Performance-only):

SizeNameTireCost
19"Gemini Wheels255/45R19Standard
20"Induction Wheels255/40R20Paid upgrade (~$2,000)

The factory tire, not just the size: your 19" Gemini wheels (the ones on this car) ship on the Continental ProContact RX (255/45R19, 104W XL), extra-load-rated with an acoustic foam inner liner (Continental's ContiSilent) specifically to quiet road noise, which carries further in a car with no engine to mask it. The 20" Induction option instead runs 255/40R20 101W/101Y XL, sourced from either Goodyear (Eagle F1 Asymmetric 5) or Michelin (Pilot Sport EV) depending on the production run. Tesla has used both for the same wheel.

Why the "XL" matters, on this tire or any replacement: EVs run heavier than comparable gas cars because of battery weight, so Tesla specs a minimum 104 load index: an XL (extra load) tire built to carry more at the same pressure than a standard-load tire in the same size. A newer HL (high load) standard exists since 2023, but XL is what your car calls for. Whatever these get replaced with, matching that load rating isn't optional the way tire brand is.

On SKUs: Tesla doesn't publish a public parts catalog the way traditional automakers do, so the "OEM part numbers" quoted on wheel-reseller and salvage listings for a casting like this aren't something Tesla itself puts out. Researching this, we found inconsistent numbers even across listings claiming to describe the same wheel. If you ever need a factory replacement, your VIN plus a Tesla Service Center or Tesla's own parts desk is the reliable path, not a part number copied off a listing site.

If you're shopping replacement tires rather than staying OEM, the common cross-shops in your size (255/45R19) split into three tiers: all-season grand-touring (Michelin CrossClimate2, Continental SecureContact AW, Goodyear Assurance WeatherReady2, Vredestein Quatrac Pro+), ultra-high-performance all-season (Michelin Pilot Sport All Season 4, Continental ExtremeContact DWS 06 Plus, Vredestein Hypertrac All Season), and summer-only performance (Michelin Pilot Sport 4, Bridgestone Potenza Sport, Vredestein Ultrac Pro). None of that is a Tesla endorsement, just what fits and gets cross-shopped in this size. The acoustic foam liner your factory tire has is a comfort nice-to-have you'd lose on most aftermarket choices, not a functional requirement.

Production history & the "best-selling car" claim

Model Y really was the best-selling vehicle on Earth in 2023: the first EV ever to hold that title. 2024 is genuinely a coin flip depending on whose numbers you trust. We checked both.

Where and when this car's design was built

  • Fremont, CA (your plant): production began January 2020; first deliveries March 13, 2020.
  • Shanghai: production began December 2020.
  • Austin, TX: trial production late 2021; official "Cyber Rodeo" opening April 7, 2022.
  • Fremont built this same body style from January 2020 until the redesigned "Juniper" version arrived in early 2025. Your 2024 car comes from near the very end of that five-year run.
  • Tesla passed 4 million cumulative global Model Y deliveries around March 2026, making it the best-selling EV nameplate in history, independent of any "best overall vehicle" argument.

Was it really the best-selling car in the world?

In 2023, yes, cleanly. JATO Dynamics, an independent auto-data firm, confirmed Model Y as the best-selling vehicle of any kind globally that year: 1.22 million units, ahead of the Toyota RAV4 and Corolla, the first time a pure EV had ever topped that list.

2024 is genuinely disputed, not a clean repeat. JATO's own 2024 count has the Toyota RAV4 narrowly ahead: 1,187,000 to Model Y's 1,185,000, a margin under 3,000 units. A different tracker, Focus2Move, counted Model Y still on top that year. Tesla's own claim of "three years running" (2023–2025) stitches together three different data vendors, one per year. Treat that framing as marketing, not an independently confirmed streak. What's not in dispute: Model Y has been the best-selling EV globally every year since 2023, no asterisk needed.

Awards this exact model year earned

  • IIHS Top Safety Pick+ for 2024, under IIHS's tougher, updated 2023+ criteria that a number of other vehicles failed to meet that cycle. Model Y has now earned this award four years running (2021–2024).
  • Consumer Reports 2024 Top Pick, EV category: the only pure battery-EV on CR's overall Top Picks list that year. Worth noting: CR has historically been one of the tougher graders of Tesla build quality, so this wasn't a rubber stamp.

Pre-Juniper vs. Juniper: what this car has and doesn't

Tesla redesigned Model Y in 2025. This car predates it: here's exactly what changed, so a buyer knows what they're not getting (and what they are).

Tesla's refreshed "Juniper" Model Y arrived for the 2025 model year, unveiled January 2025, U.S. deliveries starting March 8, 2025. Your car is a pre-refresh 2024, and the differences are concrete, not just cosmetic buzzwords:

What Juniper changed

  • Full-width LED light bars front and rear, replacing your car's separate headlight/taillight units.
  • New rear-seat touchscreen (8") for climate/media. Your car has no second screen for rear passengers.
  • Removed the gear-selector stalk: Park/Drive/Reverse moved to the touchscreen, similar to Tesla's Model 3 redesign.
  • Kept the physical turn-signal stalk, unlike the Model 3 redesign that eliminated it entirely. Your car and Juniper both still use a real stalk for turn signals.
  • Acoustic glass front and rear for lower wind noise; retuned suspension bushings reviewers describe as noticeably more settled over expansion joints.
  • EPA range rose to roughly 340+ miles, mostly from aerodynamics and efficiency work rather than a bigger battery.
One thing that did not change at launch, worth knowing: Juniper launched with the same 15.4" center screen size your car already has. A larger 16" QHD screen didn't arrive until a June 2026 running change, rolled out gradually, so plenty of early Juniper cars share your exact screen size and resolution.

Charging hardware, NACS port, and Supercharger network access are unchanged between the two generations. Nothing about how you charge today is "outdated."

What this car costs to run

Home charging is a clear, durable win over gas. Supercharging's advantage is a lot thinner than the internet tells you. At today's prices, it can vanish entirely. Here's the real math for this car's 24,000–28,000 mi/year plan.

Cost per mile: the honest comparison

Fuel sourceLowCentral estimateHigh
Home charging2.4¢~3.7¢4.4¢
Supercharging8¢~13¢20¢
Comparable gas SUV (RAV4-class)11¢ (normal gas prices)~13–14¢15¢ (today's spike)

This car's real-world efficiency runs higher than its EPA rating once you factor in highway speed and heat: call it 300–360 Wh/mile rather than the EPA-test 288. Home charging above now reflects Middle Tennessee Electric's actual residential rate schedule (effective July 2026), the utility serving Brentwood and Cool Springs: 8.1¢/kWh on the NITEFLEX off-peak plan up to 12.1¢/kWh on standard on-peak pricing. That's a real, local rate rather than a national average, and it runs meaningfully lower than an earlier national-average-based estimate did.

This car's owner doesn't have a home charger available at all: a townhouse with open, unassigned parking, not a driveway or garage, so there's no dedicated spot to install one. The home-charging row above is a reference point for buyers who do have that option, not a description of this car's real costs. Every charging figure elsewhere in this document reflects actual public charging: workplace Level 2 when it's available, Supercharging the rest of the time.
Since you'll be Supercharging regularly at your mileage, don't expect gas-to-EV savings anywhere near "half price." Supercharger pricing is dynamic and unpublished nationally. Recent data points cluster $0.35–0.45/kWh, well above the $0.25 figure still floating around online. At the high end of that range, and at pre-spike gas prices, the cost-per-mile gap between Supercharging and a gas SUV nearly disappears. Home charging is where the real, durable savings live: roughly 40–55% cheaper than gas, consistently.

Your own charging history backs this up, and then some: your first Supercharging session (10 minutes in Brentwood, TN on August 23, 2026, 20.02 kWh at $0.56/kWh, $11.21 total) actually came in above the Tesla app's own gas-equivalent estimate for that same energy: $11 spent vs. a $10 gas equivalent, per the app's own charging stats. One session isn't a trend, and $1 isn't a crisis, but it's real, dated proof the "Supercharging is always way cheaper than gas" story doesn't hold up every time. Exactly the caveat above, borne out on your own car.

Gas benchmark note: the national average sat at $4.10/gallon in late August 2026, the first time over $4 in four years, tied to a crude-oil supply shock earlier in the year. The 2026 year-to-date average is closer to $3.75. Both are reflected in the range above rather than picking one number.

Insurance

Full coverage on a Model Y runs an estimated $3,300–$4,000/year: two reputable sources landed about 20% apart, most likely reflecting state and driver-profile differences rather than a real disagreement about the car. EVs generally run 18–42% above a comparable gas SUV, mostly because of repair cost: EV collision claims average about 24% more than gas-vehicle claims, driven by proprietary body panels and the fact that almost any body work triggers an ADAS recalibration.

If you're in one of the 13 states where Tesla Insurance is offered, its usage-based Safety Score model (starts at 80, recalibrates over ~30 days of real driving) can meaningfully undercut that range for a disciplined driver, though Tesla doesn't publish flat rates, and California specifically can't use the Safety Score by state law. A newer version, Safety Score 3.0, scores every FSD-engaged mile a perfect 100 and currently operates in six of those states, Tennessee included alongside Arizona, Illinois, Indiana, Texas, and Virginia. One cited example for a driver maximizing FSD-engaged miles under that program showed a premium drop from about $380/month to about $53/month, an 86% reduction. That's one driver's result, not a guarantee, and it requires switching to Tesla Insurance plus an active FSD subscription; a standalone FSD discount without full Safety Score 3.0 participation is capped at 10%.

The federal tax credit: why it never applied to this purchase

Worth stating plainly since it comes up a lot: a used federal EV tax credit could never have applied to this car, on two independent grounds. The Used Clean Vehicle Credit required the vehicle to be at least two model years old at the time of purchase and capped the sale price at $25,000, and it stopped applying entirely to any purchase after September 30, 2025. A 2024 model-year car couldn't satisfy the "two years old" rule until 2026, by which point the credit no longer existed for any vehicle. Even setting timing aside, a used 2024 Model Y selling anywhere near real market value (currently averaging around $36,000) blows past the $25,000 cap on its own. This isn't a "credit that expired on you" story. It was never in play for this specific car, regardless of exactly when the purchase happened.

Resale value & warranty: the honest version

Model Y depreciation genuinely runs worse than the segment average, mostly because of Tesla's own price cuts. The warranty, on the other hand, is good news: it transferred to you automatically.

Depreciation: a real weak point, not a scare story

Three independent studies converge on 58–61% five-year depreciation for Model Y, against roughly 45% for the broader SUV segment and 42% for all vehicles. That's a genuine, well-documented gap, not a one-off data artifact.

  • Why: Tesla has cut new Model Y pricing by roughly 27% since mid-2022, and used prices follow those cuts fast: one documented event saw used Tesla values drop at roughly 3x the rate of the broader used market within weeks of a single new-price cut.
  • Specific to your car: ahead of the 2025 Juniper refresh, Tesla marked down outgoing pre-refresh inventory by $8,000–9,200 to clear stock: your car's generation is now competing on the used market against a newer design, which is an added headwind beyond generic "EV depreciation."
  • Current snapshot: the average used 2024 Model Y listing is around $36,378 as of August 2026, actually up 6.4% year-over-year, a live-market tick that sits in some tension with the longer depreciation curve above. Likely measuring different things (a 12-month price move vs. a 5-year age curve); we're flagging both rather than picking the one that tells a cleaner story.
Our own rough synthesis puts resale value around $14,000–20,000 at ~70,000 miles (your 2-year mileage target). No source models this exact scenario, so treat it as an order-of-magnitude placeholder. Get an actual quote (Tesla's trade-in tool, Carvana, CarMax) close to your real sale date rather than trusting this number.

Warranty: the good news

Basic vehicle4 yr / 50,000 mi
Battery & drive unit (Long Range AWD tier)8 yr / 120,000 mi, min. 70% capacity retained
Restraint system (airbags, belts)5 yr / 60,000 mi

Both the basic and battery warranties transfer automatically with the sale, to whoever buys the car: they're tied to the VIN, not the original owner, standard across the industry. No formal Tesla "re-registration" is legally required to keep the coverage valid.

There's a separate, practical step worth doing anyway: add this VIN to your own Tesla account in the app (Add Product → VIN → ID + proof of ownership; Tesla typically reviews within 3–5 business days). That's what gives you visibility into warranty/service status, the ability to schedule service, and Supercharging billed to your own payment method. It's not a legal requirement for the warranty itself, but it's the thing that makes day-to-day ownership work through the app.

FSD, Autopilot, software & connectivity: what's running

This car is running FSD (Supervised) v14.3.6, and it's confirmed active on the current owner's account: they added the $99/month subscription themselves, so there's no guessing here like there is on a lot of used-Tesla purchases. The car is also on Premium Connectivity, with the owner's phone set up as a key.

What this car has, confirmed

  • Autopilot (Autosteer + Traffic-Aware Cruise Control) is standard equipment on every Model Y, including this one, at no extra cost.
  • This car is running FSD (Supervised) v14.3.6, and the $99/month subscription is active on the current owner's account: they added it themselves, so this isn't a leftover trial from a previous owner. "Supervised" is Tesla's own term, meaning the system drives but the driver is required to stay attentive and ready to take over; it is not an unsupervised/robotaxi-grade system on this hardware.
  • The car is also subscribed to Premium Connectivity ($9.99/month, or $99/year): the paid tier above Standard Connectivity's free-for-8-years baseline. It adds satellite-view maps, live traffic visualization, in-car video and music streaming (Netflix, Disney+, Spotify and the like, each still needs its own separate app subscription), an in-car web browser, weather radar, and live Sentry Mode camera viewing from the app when away from the car. It renews next on September 21, 2026.
  • Phone Key is set up: the owner's phone unlocks and starts the car over Bluetooth automatically on approach, no card tap needed. Worth keeping a physical Key Card in the glovebox or a wallet anyway, as backup for the rare time a phone's dead or Bluetooth misbehaves.
  • Software build 2026.20.6.11 is what this car is currently on.
  • Real usage, not a subscription sitting idle: per the Tesla app's Self-Driving Stats, this car is running 81% self-driving on recent trips (64 of the last 80 miles) with a longest single FSD streak of 21.4 miles and a 2-day streak currently active.
Worth knowing for whenever you sell: your FSD subscription is tied to your Tesla account, not the VIN, so it doesn't transfer with the car. If you sell, the subscription simply ends. A buyer who wants FSD starts their own $99/month plan. That's a real difference from the old one-time-purchase model, which Tesla ended entirely on February 14, 2026: FSD bought outright before that cutoff stays with the car, VIN-tied, permanently. Premium Connectivity works the same way: it's a subscription on your account, not an asset that conveys with a sale.

This profile doesn't pull live telemetry: no real-time Autopilot mileage, streaks, or charging history. Those live inside the owner's Tesla account and the mobile app; nothing here claims to sync with them.

Real-world use cases

Specs and a VIN decode only go so far. This is what owning this specific car actually looks like against real routines and real trips, with real numbers attached: the daily commute, a weekend road trip, winter range, insurance, and a real three-jobs-one-car schedule. Built to hold more over time.

Case study: the daily commute

This car's current owner drives a fixed weekday commute from the Brentwood, TN area to Lebanon, TN: about 41 miles each way, 82 miles round trip. Departure runs 6:55–7:00am, arrival 7:34–7:40am, so the door-to-door drive is 35–40 minutes each way. Return trips leave at 5pm Monday and Tuesday, 4pm Wednesday through Friday. Home and work addresses aren't published here; the mileage and timing are what matter for the numbers below.

One constraint shapes every charging number below: this owner has no home charger. They live in a townhouse with open, unassigned parking, not a driveway or garage, so there's no dedicated spot to install one. Every charging figure in this case study reflects real public charging, workplace Level 2 and Supercharging. There's no home-charging fallback for this car.

Time

82 miles a day, 5 days a week, works out to 410 miles and roughly 6.25 hours behind the wheel every week for the commute alone, before any errands or weekend driving. Nothing about an EV changes the drive time itself: traffic is traffic. What changes is how much of that time is spent actively driving versus supervising. See "The true experience" below.

Cost: what this commute actually takes in charging

410 miles a week at this car's real-world efficiency (300–360 Wh/mile, established in What this car costs to run) works out to roughly 125–150 kWh a week for the commute alone. With no home charger available, what that costs depends on how much lands on workplace Level 2 versus Supercharging:

Charging patternPer weekPer monthBasis
Mixed: 2 days/wk Level 2 at work, rest Supercharging~$14–49~$60–214Work covers 160–240 mi/wk free; remainder at Supercharging rate
All Supercharging (no workplace charging that week)~$33–82~$142–356This car's own 8–20¢/mile Supercharging range × 410 mi
All home charging (off-peak)~$10–18~$43–78Reference only, not available to this owner: MTE's real NITEFLEX off-peak rate × 410 mi

That home-charging row is what this commute would cost with a driveway and a Level 2 charger installed, useful context for a buyer who has one, not a description of this car's real bills. This car's own first Supercharging session (see What this car costs to run) came in at $0.56/kWh, toward the high end of the Supercharging range above, so treat that row as realistic rather than optimistic.

Workplace Level 2 is the whole game here: without it, every mile defaults to Supercharging. At a typical 20–30 miles of range per hour, a 4-hour session can add 80–120 miles, more than this commute's 82-mile round trip in a single sitting. Two sessions a week can cover roughly 40–58% of the week's commuting energy at whatever the workplace charges, often free. Confirm the charging speed and rate (or that it's free) directly with the workplace; office Level 2 setups vary a lot and aren't standardized the way Supercharging is.

This owner's real charging picture: no home charger, Cool Springs as the backstop

This is this car's actual situation, not a hypothetical for a different kind of buyer. Cool Springs, TN, has a dense cluster of public charging nearby, Superchargers and third-party stations around the retail corridor, which is what makes the no-home-charger reality workable rather than a dealbreaker. The optimization questions are cost and time, not access:

  • Charge to 80%, not 100%, on a normal week. Charging speed drops sharply past 80% on any lithium-ion pack, so the last 20% takes disproportionately long for not much extra range. Save 100% charges for actual road trips.
  • Stack charging on top of something else already happening. Cool Springs' Superchargers sit at retail centers, so a 20–30 minute charge during a grocery run or errand costs zero extra time out of the day.
  • Navigate to the Supercharger through the car's own trip planner rather than driving there directly. Routing through the car's navigation preconditions the battery for faster charging on arrival, especially in cold weather.
  • Without workplace Level 2 that week, budget for the all-Supercharging end of the table above: roughly $142–356 a month for this specific commute, before any other driving.

The real question without a home charger isn't whether this works, it's how often the car actually needs to plug in. Running this commute's own numbers (24% battery = 87 miles one morning, the same real data point used below) forward across a work week, starting from an 80% charge and losing about 22.6% a day to the round trip:

DayZero mid-week chargingOne mid-week top-up (Tue night)
Mon80% → 57%80% → 57%
Tue57% → 35%57% → 35%, recharges to 80% that night
Wed35% → 12%80% → 57%
Thu12% → runs out57% → 35%
Frialready out of range35% → 12%

Zero mid-week charging runs this car out before Thursday's drive home. One mid-week stop, Tuesday night is a natural choice given Cool Springs' retail-corridor Superchargers, keeps the whole week above a reasonable margin, ending Friday around 12%. That's the real cadence without a home charger: roughly two charging sessions a week, not a nightly ritual. A different rhythm than a driveway owner's, but a manageable one.

Adapters worth buying

  • CCS1-to-NACS adapter (~$200 from Tesla's own shop, or a ~$230 installed bundle on some Model 3/Y configurations): opens up non-Tesla DC fast chargers (Electrify America, EVgo, and similar), which matters more in a charging-dense area with multiple networks nearby than it does for someone who only ever uses Superchargers.
  • J1772 adapter, for non-Tesla Level 2 stations: what ships in the frunk or glovebox has changed across model years, so check there first before buying a duplicate. If it's missing, Tesla's own shop sells one.

Battery care for a commuter without a home charger

  • Charging to 80% in fewer, larger public sessions is still a healthy pattern, per Tesla's own guidance, a different rhythm than a driveway owner's nightly top-up, but not a worse one. Roughly two sessions a week, the cadence worked out above, keeps this pack comfortably inside the range Tesla recommends for daily use.
  • Charging to 100% occasionally, before a longer trip, is fine. Living at 100% or routinely running the pack down near empty is what actually stresses it over years, not the size of any single charging session.
  • Relying on DC fast charging instead of slow overnight charging is a real tradeoff, not a free one: Supercharging twice a week is somewhat harder on a pack over many years than a nightly trickle would be, though Tesla's thermal management (see winter range, below) mitigates most of it. It's a reasonable cost of not having a home charger, not something to worry over on a car this new.
  • A concrete illustration from this car: at 24% and 87 miles of rated range one morning, with a 41-mile drive to work ahead, that leaves about 46 miles of buffer on arrival, but only about 5 miles of buffer if driving straight home again without charging at all that day. That's the real margin this owner manages without a driveway to fall back on.

Supercharging membership: what's actually available

There's no discounted Supercharging plan available to Tesla owners. Tesla's $12.99/month membership exists specifically for non-Tesla EVs to access the Supercharger network at a reduced per-kWh rate; Tesla vehicles already charge at the standard member-equivalent rate by default, so there's nothing extra to subscribe to. The honest weekly budget for this commute, without a home charger to fall back on, lands around $14–49 in a week when workplace Level 2 comes through, or $33–82 in a week when it doesn't.

The true experience: what FSD actually changes on this drive

Per this car's own Self-Driving Stats (see FSD, software & connectivity), FSD is engaged for 81% of recent miles driven. Applied to this specific commute's roughly 6.25 hours a week behind the wheel, that's on the order of 5 hours a week where the car is handling the steering, braking, and lane-and-turn decisions on a route it drives every day, while the driver supervises rather than actively operates. "Supervised" is the operative word: this isn't an unsupervised or hands-off system, and attention is still required throughout. What it changes is the kind of effort, active moment-to-moment driving versus monitoring, on a route repetitive enough that the difference is felt daily rather than occasionally.

FSD value: short-term versus long-term

Short-term, the value shows up as reduced fatigue on a repetitive, unavoidable drive: less continuous steering and pedal input on the same predictable roads, five days a week. Long-term, the value compounds two ways. FSD ships as a subscription tied to this car's current account rather than the VIN (see FSD, software & connectivity), so its cost is a monthly decision, not a sunk one, and it can be dropped or restarted as priorities change. And because the underlying hardware is confirmed HW4 (see This car, verified), this specific car is positioned to receive whatever capability improvements Tesla ships to that hardware generation going forward, on a commute where more capability has a daily, not occasional, payoff.

Vehicle comparison: gas, hybrid, and this Model Y

This car's owner briefly owned a Lexus ES300h (hybrid), five days, before switching to this Model Y. For a same-model, gas-only reference point, the Lexus ES350 is the ES300h's own non-hybrid sibling trim, same platform, different powertrain, which makes it a cleaner comparison than picking an unrelated gas vehicle.

VehicleFuelEPA combinedWeekly fuel cost, this commute
Lexus ES350 (gas)Gasoline25 mpg~$106–141/wk*
Lexus ES300h (hybrid)Gasoline44 mpg$60–80/wk (owner-reported)
This Model Y (electric)Electricity300–360 Wh/mi, real-world~$14–49/wk, no home charger: workplace L2 + Supercharging

*Estimated by scaling the ES300h's own reported gas cost by the mpg gap between the two Lexus trims: 44 mpg vs. 25 mpg means the ES350 burns roughly 1.76x more fuel for the same driving. Not an independently reported figure.

Fuel and charging aren't the only running cost that differs by powertrain. The Department of Energy and Argonne National Laboratory's own maintenance-cost research puts EVs at roughly 6¢/mile to maintain against 10¢/mile for a comparable gas car and 9¢/mile for a hybrid, mostly fewer fluids, no exhaust system, and regenerative braking that extends brake life. Applied to this commute's 21,320 miles a year, that's a real, if secondary, advantage on top of the fuel numbers above: roughly $1,279 a year in maintenance for this Model Y against $2,132 for the ES350 and $1,919 for the ES300h.

Cost analysis: Model Y vs. two alternatives

This car's owner briefly owned a Lexus ES300h, five days, before switching to this Model Y with FSD. Laid out side by side, using the owner's own real payment figures:

VehiclePaymentFuel / chargingTotal monthly outgo
Lexus ES300h (hybrid)$660/mo$260–347/mo (gas, owner-reported $60–80/wk)~$920–1,007
This Model Y w/ FSD$900/mo, all-in incl. FSD~$80–325/mo (this car's full driving, no home charger)~$980–1,225
Lexus ES350 (gas-only reference)~$660/mo, assumed~$457–610/mo (gas, scaled from ES300h)~$1,117–1,270

The ES350's payment is assumed equal to the ES300h's for a clean comparison; new pricing on the gas-only trim typically runs somewhat lower than the hybrid, so if anything this understates the real gap between the ES350 and the other two options. The Model Y's charging range is wider than the commute-only figures earlier in this section because it covers this car's full driving, roughly 24,000–28,000 mi/year: the low end assumes workplace Level 2 covers what it can, two days a week when it's available; the high end leans more heavily on Supercharging in weeks it isn't. There's no home-charging floor to narrow that range the way there would be for a buyer with a driveway.

The honest answer to "how much is Supercharging per month": this owner has no home charger at all, a townhouse with open, unassigned parking rather than a driveway or garage, so the real choice is how much of the year's driving lands on free-or-cheap workplace Level 2 versus full-price Supercharging. All-Supercharging across this car's full driving pattern runs $160–467 a month; with workplace Level 2 covering what it can, that drops to roughly $80–325 a month. There's no $125–180 home-charging floor available here the way there would be for someone with a driveway.

Lined up this way, the honest read partly matches what this car's owner originally expected, and partly doesn't: the hybrid lands close to $1,000 a month either way, $920–1,007. The Model Y runs from close to that same number when workplace charging comes through, $980, up to meaningfully more in a stretch where it doesn't, $1,225. Short-term, it's close to a wash when the charging mix cooperates, and a real gap when it doesn't, not a clean win either way regardless.

The real asymmetry still shows up after the loan. Once the Model Y is paid off or refinanced down, its ongoing cost drops to roughly its charging cost alone: $80–325 a month for this owner specifically, with no home-charging floor to anchor the low end. A paid-off gas or hybrid car doesn't get that same drop: the ES300h keeps costing $260–347 a month in gas indefinitely, and the ES350 keeps costing $457–610 a month, for as long as it's driven. That gap, not the monthly payment while both are still financed, is where the EV's financial case actually lives, narrower than it would be with a home charger, but still real.

But per this car's owner, that's not actually the deciding factor. With the total monthly outgo in the same range either way, the real advantage cited was FSD itself: on a commute like the one above, roughly 5 hours a week of supervised driving, that adds up to increased productivity and decreased stress that a spreadsheet comparison doesn't capture. The financial case landing close, even without the cheapest possible charging setup, is what made room for that to be the deciding factor, not proof that it was the only one.

Case study: a weekend road trip

The commute above is home-charged daily driving, where this car's cost advantage is clear and consistent. A genuine road trip changes that math. Take a common trip from this area: Nashville to Gulf Shores, AL, a well-worn weekend and vacation drive, roughly 460 miles one way from the Brentwood area, most of it on I-65 South, then I-10 East, then local parkways into Gulf Shores and Orange Beach. A real source puts the Nashville-anchored version of this drive at about 470 miles and a little over 7 hours of driving; starting from Brentwood, a few miles closer to the interstate, trims that slightly.

Charging stops: the real math

This car's comfortable real-world range between fast-charging stops, running the same 20–80% pattern recommended for the commute (see above), lands somewhere around 250–270 miles at highway speed. A 460-mile leg needs roughly two Supercharging stops each way, about 25–35 minutes apiece for a 20–80% top-up on this platform. The route has real coverage the whole way: Superchargers exist along I-65 in Athens and Huntsville near the state line, Birmingham further south, and a Supercharger sits at The Wharf in Orange Beach, right at the destination. The car's own trip planner would pick the actual two stops from stations like these rather than this being a fixed, pre-mapped route.

Time: this trip against a comparable gas car

Door to door, that's roughly 7–7.5 hours of driving plus 50–70 minutes of charging, call it 8–8.5 hours total. A comparable gas car covers the same distance in the same 7–7.5 hours of driving plus one short fuel stop, 10–15 minutes. For a trip this length, the honest time cost of going electric is somewhere around 45 minutes to an hour, not nothing, but not the multi-hour ordeal it's sometimes made out to be either.

Cost: where the math actually flips

920 miles round trip at this car's real-world 300–360 Wh/mile works out to roughly 276–331 kWh. At this car's own real Supercharging rate of $0.56/kWh, that's roughly $155–185 for the whole round trip. Run the same 920 miles through the ES300h at 44 mpg and Tennessee's $3.64/gallon average, and gas comes to about $76. Through the gas-only ES350 at 25 mpg, about $134. For a Supercharging-heavy long trip specifically, this car can cost more to run than either gas comparator, not less. That's the flip side of the home-charging advantage documented in What this car costs to run: the savings live at home, on the commute, at the lower, off-peak rate. On the road, paying full Supercharging price for every mile, the advantage isn't guaranteed, and here it disappears entirely.

Case study: winter range

Everything above assumes mild-weather driving. Cold weather is real and worth accounting for honestly, using published data rather than guessing, since this car doesn't have a full winter of its own logged range data yet.

Recurrent's analysis of 30,000-plus real vehicles, using fleet telematics rather than a lab test, found EVs retain about 78% of maximum range at 32°F and roughly 70% at 20°F. Tesla specifically is called out as one of the stronger performers in that data set, largely because of the Octovalve thermal system Tesla introduced in the Model Y in 2021, which this 2024 car has. That means these percentages are closer to a conservative floor for this specific car than a precise prediction: it likely does somewhat better than the fleet-wide average, not worse.

ConditionRange retainedApplied to this car's 310-mi EPA rating
Mild weather (baseline)100%310 mi
~32°F~78%~242 mi
~20°F~70%~217 mi

Against the 82-mile round-trip commute above, even the 20°F figure leaves a wide margin; cold weather doesn't meaningfully threaten a commute this short. It matters more on the road trip case study above: at 217–242 miles of cold-weather range instead of the 250–270-mile mild-weather estimate used there, the same 460-mile leg would realistically need three to four Supercharging stops each way instead of two, adding real time to an already-longer winter drive.

Case study: insurance versus the ES300h

This car's own insurance estimate, from What this car costs to run, is $3,300–4,000/year for full coverage. Two independent sources put full-coverage insurance on a Lexus ES300h meaningfully lower: about $2,200–3,033/year, depending on trim and driver profile, using comparable driver assumptions (a driver in their 40s, clean record, full coverage, roughly 12,000–13,000 miles a year).

This is another place the EV doesn't have the advantage. The gap tracks the same reason already documented in the running-costs section: EV collision claims average around 24% more than gas-vehicle claims, driven by proprietary body panels and ADAS recalibration triggered by almost any body work. A hybrid sedan with a longer safety record and simpler repairs insures for less, consistently.

The one lever that can close some of that gap: Tesla Insurance, where available (13 states as of this car's own research), prices on a usage-based Safety Score rather than a flat vehicle-class rate. Tennessee is also one of six states with the newer Safety Score 3.0, which scores FSD-engaged miles a perfect 100 and showed one driver's premium drop from about $380 to about $53 a month; see What this car costs to run for the full caveats. California specifically can't use either version by state law, and Tesla doesn't publish flat numbers to compare in advance.

Case study: three jobs, one car

This case study generalizes a real, current situation: a single man in his mid-40s, starting over after a divorce, running three things at once on the same car. A day job with the same Brentwood-to-Lebanon commute covered above. A software business, built at night. And weekend gig driving on top of both. The numbers below are what a schedule like that actually asks of a vehicle, and of the person driving it.

Weekdays: the job by day, the business by night

The weekday commute itself, 82 miles round trip to Lebanon, is already covered in full in the daily commute case study above; the cost, the charging pattern, and the FSD numbers there are this same schedule's foundation. What changes here is what happens after the drive home: the day doesn't end, a second job starts. Evenings go to running a real software business: Paddock20 (paddock20.com), an agentic engineering studio doing custom development and AI automation for other companies, which closed about $2,000 in new business in a single recent week. The FSD "true experience" finding from the commute case study, reduced micro-fatigue rather than reduced responsibility, matters more on a day like this than on an average one: less of the drive's mental load carried into a night of work that needs its own full attention.

What changed: a work van, then a five-day Lexus, then this car

This exact commute has run in three different vehicles. Before this car, the same 41-mile-each-way drive was done in a 2015 Chevrolet Express 2500 cargo van, 4.8L V8, EPA-rated at 11 city / 17 highway mpg. On a mostly-highway commute like this one, real-world economy for a loaded work van in that range typically lands around 13 to 15 mpg, short of the full highway number. A Lexus ES300h briefly followed, owned five days before switching to this Model Y; the financial comparison against the ES300h elsewhere in this document (see What this car costs to run) uses that car's real numbers regardless of how briefly it was actually owned. Five days is a short window, but it's enough to anchor the real numbers used here.

VehicleFuelWeekly cost, this commute
Before2015 Chevrolet Express 2500 (4.8L V8)Gasoline~$102–129
Now2024 Tesla Model YElectricity~$14–49

Weekends: more coding, plus Instacart

Weekends carry the heaviest load: more software development time, plus Instacart shifts fit around it, Friday 7 to 9pm, Saturday 11am to 3pm, Sunday 10am to 1pm, nine hours a week of gig driving in the Brentwood area on top of everything else. Instacart shopper pay is well documented, roughly $15 to $25 an hour including tips, but reliable per-shift mileage data isn't; this document isn't going to invent a number for miles driven on these specific shifts where none exists. What's real: those nine hours are additional driving on top of the commute, most likely already folded into this car's own established 24,000–28,000 mile annual plan (see What this car costs to run) rather than an uncounted cost this section is missing.

This is where FSD compounds hardest. The road trip and winter range case studies above are about trips that happen a few times a year. This one is about every single week, indefinitely, for someone with less spare time and mental bandwidth than almost any other profile this document could describe. The FSD value already established for the daily commute, roughly five hours a week of supervised rather than fully active driving, shows up most clearly on a schedule like this: arriving home with something left for the second job, instead of already spent. That's not a claim this document can put a dollar figure on, and it shouldn't try to. But it's the most honest version yet of the thesis this document keeps coming back to: the financial case for this car is close enough to a wash that time and attention end up deciding it, and for a schedule like this one, time and attention are the whole game.

Looking ahead: resale at the two-year mark

This isn't a full case study yet, because the numbers don't exist yet. This car sits at 19,420 miles against a 2-year, 50,000–56,000-added-mile target, meaning it's still early in that window. The Resale value & warranty section already projects $14,000–20,000 at that mileage, based on today's depreciation curves. When this car actually reaches that point, this section is where a real, not projected, resale case study belongs.

Gone from your car specifically

The Atari arcade classics (Missile Command, Asteroids, Lunar Lander and the rest) were removed in June 2024 specifically from vehicles with AMD Ryzen infotainment. Your 2024 Model Y almost certainly has that hardware, so don't go looking for them; the current Arcade lineup rotates other titles (Cuphead, Beach Buggy Racing 2, Stardew Valley among them).

Also worth correcting: light-up, auto-presenting door handles are a popular aftermarket accessory, not something Tesla actually ships from the factory. If you've seen that on another car, it wasn't stock software.

Things experienced owners find embarrassingly late

  • Trip Planner auto-preconditioning: navigating to a Supercharger automatically warms the battery pack so it hits peak charge speed the moment you plug in, estimated to save up to 10 minutes per stop. A December 2025 update added live stall occupancy to the map.
  • Tesla Theater streaming (Netflix, YouTube, Disney+, Hulu, Twitch): requires the car fully parked with the parking brake set: it does not work while driving, and doesn't turn on just because Autopilot or FSD is engaged, despite that being a common assumption.
  • In-car web browser: a real browser in the app dock, useful at a Supercharger stop. A 2026 update added full-screen support and even browser-based video calling.
  • Naming your car in the app isn't just cosmetic: certain names (Monty Python and Hitchhiker's Guide references among them) trigger their own hidden responses.
Not yet on this car, for what it's worth: the newest door-open "TESLA" wordmark animation that debuted in a mid-2026 software update is limited to 2024+ Model 3 and the redesigned Juniper Model Y. Something to look forward to if you ever upgrade, not something missing from your current software.

Accessories that earn their keep

Tesla ships this car with almost no cargo organization and no floor protection. Here's what owners buy first, and a few places to compare before you do.

Where to start looking

Tesery (tesery.com) is a dedicated Tesla accessories store that's been running since 2021, with a Model Y catalog split by generation, so it's easy to find parts sized for a legacy car instead of a Juniper one. It's one option, not the only one. Tesla's own shop (shop.tesla.com) sells OEM parts at OEM prices with guaranteed fit. Teslarati's shop is another Tesla-focused storefront worth comparing against before you buy. None of this is an endorsement of one seller over another. Treat it as a starting point for comparison shopping.

What owners buy first

Roughly in the order most owners buy them, based on what comes up most in owner forums and shows up as bestsellers at the stores above:

  • All-weather floor liners: the single most common first purchase. The factory carpet has no protection at all, and liners trimmed to the Model Y footwell keep road salt and mud off it.
  • Frunk and trunk organizers: the car ships with no cargo organization anywhere, front or back. Fitted bins stop groceries and gear from sliding around both trunks.
  • Center console tray: the console's open storage tunnel is deep but unshaped, so small items slide around and disappear into it. A fitted insert fixes that.
  • Windshield and rear sunshades: closer to necessary than optional on a car with this much glass overhead. Interior temperatures climb fast without one.
  • Center screen protector: the 15.4" display handles nearly every control in the car, so it takes constant touch contact. A matte or glass protector is cheap insurance against scratches.
Skip anything that changes the exterior lighting, badging, or aero pieces if resale matters. Those are the easiest changes for a future buyer to flag as not stock, and the cheapest to leave alone.
+

Living with a transportation appliance

This car's owner coined that phrase because it fits: mainly a commuter, built to run every day without asking for much back.

What you notice in the first week

  • Full torque from a stop, cold or not: electric motors don't need to warm up the way a gas engine does. The power is there the instant you press the pedal, even on the coldest morning of the year.
  • The cabin is ready before you are: start the climate from the app and it's already comfortable by the time you're in the seat, no idling in the driveway first.
  • One-pedal driving: regenerative braking handles most of the slowing down in stop-and-go traffic, and it's part of why the physical brake pads last so much longer than a gas car's.
  • Updates show up on their own: new capability can arrive overnight with no shop visit.
  • Real cargo room: 34.3 cubic feet behind the rear seats, 76.2 with them folded flat, plus a separate 4.1 cubic foot frunk up front. Enough to move a mattress or a week of gear without a roof box.

What other owners end up telling you

  • The frunk has a drain plug. It's a documented feature, not a workaround: pull it and the frunk can be hosed out, or packed with ice as a cooler on a road trip.
  • Controls → Charging has a "Keep Accessory Power On" toggle. Switch it on and the 12V and USB outlets stay powered, down to 20% battery, without Sentry Mode needing to run at all. Useful for a dashcam or a cooler overnight.
  • Camp Mode turns the back seat into somewhere to sleep. Fold the seats flat, run Camp Mode, and it holds cabin temperature and keeps the interior lit off the battery instead of a running engine.
  • Dog Mode is real, and most non-owners don't believe it. Leave the dog, and the AC keeps running while the center screen shows the cabin temperature for anyone who walks by and worries.
  • Windows crack open from the app. On a hot day, you can vent the car before you're anywhere near it, without fully unlocking it.
None of this is unique to this specific car: it's what the Long Range AWD platform does for anyone driving one, legacy or Juniper. What makes it feel like an appliance instead of a car is that most of it runs in the background, without being asked.

Forums, third-party apps that go further than the Tesla app, what it actually takes to self-host TeslaMate, and the handful of YouTube channels the community trusts for straight information over hype.

TeslaMate, and the newer AI-assistant layer on top

The table above calls TeslaMate "free, self-hosted, for the technically inclined." Here's what that means in practice, since it's a meaningfully different commitment than downloading TezLab or starting a Tessie subscription.

TeslaMate runs as a small server stack: the TeslaMate application itself, a Postgres database to store everything it pulls, Grafana to turn that data into dashboards, and an MQTT broker (Mosquitto) if the data is going to feed something like Home Assistant. All four run together through Docker, on a machine that stays on and connected to the internet continuously, not a laptop that sleeps. A Raspberry Pi 3 or newer on a 64-bit OS works, so does a Docker-capable NAS, a spare always-on computer, or a small cloud VM. The floor is 1 GB of RAM, with 2 GB recommended.

The part most people worry about first: does this mean handing a Tesla login to a third party? It doesn't, and it's worth being specific about why. Personal, single-car use doesn't require registering anything with Tesla's Developer or Fleet API program; that's specifically for Tesla's commercial fleet customers, and Tesla's own Fleet API logs at a coarser resolution than individual owners actually want anyway. TeslaMate authenticates through the unofficial Owner API instead, the same reverse-engineered API much of the Tesla third-party app world is built on. The standard tool for generating that token, Tesla Auth, built by TeslaMate's own original author, opens Tesla's real login page in a native window, MFA included, and hands over the resulting access and refresh tokens to paste into TeslaMate afterward. The password itself goes to Tesla directly, never to TeslaMate or the token tool.

Get it from the source, nothing else. TeslaMate's own maintainers warn that impersonator websites and unofficial mobile apps using its name have shown up before, some carrying malware. The only versions worth trusting are the official GitHub repository (teslamate-org/teslamate) and its documentation (docs.teslamate.org). Anywhere else offering a shortcut is the sign to stop.

There's a newer layer on top of either data source, and it's specifically what prompted this section: letting an AI assistant query, or in one case act on, this car's data directly, through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). TezLab now offers this as an official, hosted feature gated behind TezLab Pro, listed on the App Store at $6.99 a month or $59.99 a year (pricing can vary slightly by platform and region), with a one-time-payment Founders Series membership as the alternative. Connect it to Claude or any other MCP-compatible assistant through OAuth, no server required, and it can read charging reports, battery health, drive patterns, and efficiency data, plus send real commands to the car itself, gated behind a confirmation step. TeslaMate has its own answer to the same idea, unofficial and community-maintained: an open-source MCP server that reads straight from a self-hosted TeslaMate's own database, free, with no subscription attached, but strictly read-only, no command capability at all, and one more piece of software layered onto the stack described above.

The dividing line worth sitting with: an AI assistant reading this car's data is a fairly low-stakes decision either way. An AI assistant sending real commands to the car, even gated behind a confirmation step, is a different kind of decision, worth making deliberately rather than defaulting into by clicking through an OAuth prompt.

What either path would actually change about this document: every charging and resale figure above is a model, built from published rates and this car's own spot-check numbers, one real Supercharging session, one real week's charging pattern, not a running total. A real logger, TeslaMate or otherwise, replaces the model with the real thing: every charge and every drive logged as it happens, plus a battery degradation curve tracked against this car's actual miles instead of the generic depreciation curve the resale estimate leans on now.

Given the technical work already behind Paddock20, standing up the self-hosted stack is a smaller lift here than for most owners. TeslaMate itself is free; the real ongoing cost is one more always-on system to keep patched, on top of everything else already on this owner's plate.

Forums

  • Tesla Owners Online: 51,000+ members, especially active on software-build discussion.
  • r/teslamotors (~2M members) for general news and technical Q&A; r/TeslaLounge (~93,000) for the more casual, lifestyle side.
  • Tesla's own official forums (forums.tesla.com), where staff occasionally weigh in.

YouTube channels known for accuracy over hype

  • Tesla Daily (Rob Maurer): near-daily, data-driven news and analysis.
  • Out of Spec Reviews (Kyle Conner): rigorous, brand-agnostic range and winter testing.
  • State of Charge (Tom Moloughney): more depth on home/AC charging than any other channel we found.
  • DirtyTesla: unedited, real-world FSD test drives, not curated highlight reels.

A little trivia

The S-3-X-Y model naming is confirmed intentional. Elon Musk has said it directly. The "3" exists only because Ford already held the trademark on Tesla's original choice, "Model E."

A note on honesty

Every figure above is sourced and dated as of August 2026 rather than assumed from memory. Tesla changes pricing, range ratings, and software constantly. Where sources disagreed or a number couldn't be pinned down precisely, we said so instead of picking whichever looked cleaner. This is a reference, not official Tesla documentation. Always confirm anything financially or mechanically significant against your own account, window sticker, or door-jamb placard.
